title: Behold the vampire camel, the fanged beast that once roamed North America

Despite its 'sexy name,' Vampyrocamelus was no blood-sucking fiend
You have nothing to fear from the vampire camel.
For one thing, it's been roughly 12 million years since this fanged creature roamed the plains of what is now North America.
And despite its two sets of Dracula-like teeth and monstrous nickname, it was, in all likelihood, a leaf-munching herbivore, not a blood-sucking fiend.
"Unless you'd done something to make it mad, it wouldn't bother you at all," paleontologist Donald Prothero told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal. "We just thought he deserved a sexy name."

As It Happens6:29The vampire camel roamed North America millions of years ago. But it's not as scary as it sounds

Vampyrocamelus is one of five newly described species identified in a massive monograph on the evolution of North American camels, published in the New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science Bulletins.

Scientists say the discovery sheds new light on what life was like during the Clarendonian period, when giant predators and herds of grazing mammals roamed savannah-like grasslands of what is now North America.
What are those teeth for?
The vampire camel made its home between 12 and 13 million years ago in what is now Texas, Oklahoma and Nebraska.
Only the males sported the large, curved fangs from which it earns its name.
Despite those pointy front chompers, molars recovered from Vampyrocamelus fossils suggest that, like all camels, it was an herbivore.
Fossils from Vampyrocamelus reveal two sets of curved canines. (Donald Prothero)
So if those teeth weren't made for shredding the flesh of unwitting prey, what were they for?

"Male camels use their teeth to fight each other and bite each other until one of them dominates and then he gets to be the father of all the next generation," said Prothero, an adjunct professor at California State Polytechnic University, Pomona.
In fact, Prothero says, it's common for male camels to have more pronounced canines than females. But in modern species, they're more conical and much less obvious.

"The males of modern camels use them to fight among themselves," Prothero said. "And I'm told that one of the things they do most often when they're fighting with their sharp teeth is to bite each other's testicles."
Camels in North America?
Today's camels live in the deserts of Africa and Asia, and the mountains of South America. But that hasn't always been so.
Prothero says camels first evolved in North America about 46 million years ago. And since 1982, he's made it his mission to document every camel species on the continent.

To do that, he and his colleagues and students have been analyzing fossils from the Frick collection, which consists of roughly 200,000 specimens spread across seven floors at the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH) in New York.
There's an entire floor dedicated to camels, Prothero says, comprising 20,000 specimens.
"It's mostly just drawers and drawers and draws of skulls and jaws and limb bones," Prothero said. "Some of them have been in that collection for 100 years and no one really studied them yet."

blocks.text: That's because it was originally the private collection of millionaire Childs Frick.
Until Fick died in 1965, his collection was off-limits to scientists outside his employ. It would be another decade before the collection was moved to New York and made accessible to researchers.

Prothero and his colleagues pored through that collection and categorized 80 species of North American camels across 40 genuses, including five that are new to science, including a long-snouted camel called Longirostrotylopus holroydae.
The researchers also scrapped 130 previously identified species that are no longer considered valid in light of new evolutionary information.
Longirostrotylopus holroydae is a newly described genus and species of long-snouted camel from the John Day Fossil Beds of Oregon. (Submitted by Donald Prothero)
Danielle Fraser, a paleobiologist at the Canadian Museum of Nature, welcomed this new taxonomy, including the vampire camel.
"If we don't know how many species there were, we may fail to reveal true patterns of evolutionary change," Fraser, who was not involved in the research, said in an email
"This monograph could help improve fossil databases that are used by numerous scientists to understand how mammalian faunas have changed through time."
Interview with Donald Prothero produced by Nishat Chowdhury
